name: Sweep (orchestrated)
description: Release sweep as a decomposed block tree instead of one linear prompt: parallel read-only analysis (hunk attribution, unclaimed-file triage) produces a commit plan, then a SERIAL roster-complete loop cuts one commit per changelog entry. The mechanical half of planning is carried by two release-agnostic scripts (scripts/release_plan.py index; scripts/release_hunks.py dump/split/merge) so the agent records hunk attribution as a {hunk: entry} mapping instead of hand-writing diffs, and every patch is validated with git apply --cached --check before any commit stage sees it. The announce stages (GitHub Release, Slack) are gated on the push being verified in git - tag present, branch not ahead, HEAD is the bump commit - so nothing is announced for a release that did not land. Escalation is confined to the blocks that mutate: the commit loop and residue sweep need git add/rm/commit (plus git apply to stage a split hunk set), the changelog and bump steps need to write CHANGELOG.md and the version files, the push step needs git push, and the GitHub Release step needs gh. The analysis half asks for nothing that mutates - its only grant is 'git apply --cached --check', a validate-only form that cannot touch the index - and the tag step needs git tag, whose read-only floor lists and verifies tags but no longer creates them. No grant anywhere admits reset, checkout, clean, rebase or a forced push.

body.name: Release invariants
body.state_context:
You are one stage of an automated release sweep for this repository. Standing givens for every stage:

ERRORS vs AMBIGUITY. An error is a command that actually failed (non-zero exit, merge conflict, rejected push) - report it and fail your block. Ambiguity, judgment calls, an incomplete changelog, untracked files, and 'which version?' are NOT errors: the rules below already decide them. Never end your turn asking the operator to choose.

THE LEDGER IS THE RECORD. All cross-stage state lives in .ziya/sweep/ledger.json (writable, no permission needed). Read it first, write it last. Do not rely on prose from a previous stage for anything you can read out of the ledger - your conversation is sandboxed and discarded, the ledger is not.

GROUPING RULE. One commit per changelog entry. The '- ' entries in the '## [Unreleased]' section of CHANGELOG.md ARE the enumeration of this release's logical changes. Two entries share a commit only when one indivisible hunk carries both. Sharing a file is NOT a reason to combine - separate hunks in one file stage independently and that is the ordinary case. The entry list is a FLOOR, not the whole roster: a changed file with no entry yet still gets its own group.

VERSION RULE. LAST_RELEASED is the highest tag matching vX.Y.Z[.W]. FILE_VERSION is pyproject.toml (canonical if version files disagree). If FILE_VERSION > LAST_RELEASED a human already bumped it - TARGET = FILE_VERSION exactly, including a rollover ending in .0. Otherwise TARGET = LAST_RELEASED with the final segment + 1. Never leave a gap above LAST_RELEASED.

EXCLUSION RULE. Tracked modifications are always in scope. An untracked file is in scope only if committed code references it or it already has an Unreleased entry. Any other untracked file or new package is in-progress work: exclude it and record the reason. Always exclude gitignored paths - note that .ziya/ is gitignored in this repo, so nothing under it is ever committable no matter what a changelog entry says about it.

CHANGELOG RULE. '## [Unreleased]' is the only place entries go. Numbered version sections are published and must never be modified. Each of Added / Fixed / Changed / Removed / Security appears AT MOST ONCE per version section, with every entry of that category under it.

ANNOUNCE RULE. Nothing is posted to any external surface (GitHub Release, Slack) until the release is verified pushed FROM GIT: the tag exists, the branch is not ahead of its upstream, and HEAD is the version-bump commit. The ledger's mode and an earlier stage's prose are hints, not evidence - a stage that narrated a failed push without failing its block must not be able to trigger an announcement. If the gate fails, post nothing and fail.

TOOLING. Two release-agnostic scripts carry the mechanical half of planning so the judgement is recorded as data rather than as hand-written diffs: `python3 scripts/release_plan.py index` builds the entry/path index (stable slug entry_ids, claimed / contended / unclaimed partition, dropped citations) straight from CHANGELOG.md and `git status`; `python3 scripts/release_hunks.py dump|split|merge` lists a contended file's hunks by number, turns a {hunk index: entry_id} mapping into per-entry patches validated with `git apply --cached --check`, and records a merge escape with its reason. Neither names a version, a file or an entry; neither touches the index or the working tree.

body.name: P0 - Reconcile any interrupted run
body.instructions:
Decide whether this is a fresh sweep or a resume, and write the answer into the ledger so no later stage has to re-derive it.

Read {{var.ledger}}. A missing file means fresh - create it. If it exists, a previous run was interrupted; RECONCILE it against git rather than trusting it. The ledger is a hint, not the record: a stage may have completed work and died before recording it, so an unrecorded group is NOT evidence the work is undone.

For each group the ledger lists as incomplete, check whether its files still appear in `git status --porcelain`. If they do not, that group is already committed - mark it done. Verify against `git log $(git describe --tags --abbrev=0)..HEAD --oneline`.

Re-derive the lowest incomplete phase from git state, not from the ledger:
  - commits incomplete if `git status --porcelain` still lists in-scope tracked modifications
  - changelog/bump incomplete if no `chore: bump version to X.Y.Z` commit exists for the target, or CHANGELOG.md still has a '## [Unreleased]' header holding this release's entries
  - tag incomplete if `git tag -l vX.Y.Z` is empty
  - push incomplete if `git status -sb` shows the branch ahead of upstream

Re-triage the exclusion list from scratch. Any list a previous run recorded may have been enumerated once and never revisited, so it can name fewer paths than are currently untracked. Collect every '??' entry from `git status --porcelain` and hand the whole set forward - the triage stage will classify them. Pay particular attention to untracked modules that committed code references: grep for the module path and bare filename including `require(...)` and `import` under frontend/src. A committed reference to an uncommitted module is a release blocker even inside try/catch, because bundlers resolve specifiers at build time, so it breaks in a clean checkout while the author's tree builds fine.

Write the reconciled ledger back to {{var.ledger}} with keys: mode ('fresh' or 'resume'), resume_phase, groups_done, exclusions. Then emit_artifact a data part named "resume" holding {"mode": ..., "resume_phase": ..., "groups_done": <count>} and state in prose what you reconciled and what you are skipping.

body.name: P1 - Survey and decide the target version
body.instructions:
Survey the release and fix the target version. Read-only - commit nothing.

Run `git status --porcelain`, `git diff --stat`, `git diff --cached --stat`, `git describe --tags --abbrev=0` and `git tag -l --sort=-v:refname` (first few). Read the version out of pyproject.toml.

Apply the VERSION RULE from your standing context to compute TARGET. Do not ask which version to use - the rule decides. State the inputs you used and the branch of the rule you took, so the decision is auditable.

Count, and report, three numbers because they size every later stage: total changed paths, tracked modifications, untracked paths.

Append a 'release' object to {{var.ledger}} with target_version, last_released_tag, file_version and those three counts. Then emit_artifact a data part named "release" holding {"target_version": "X.Y.Z", "last_released_tag": "vX.Y.Z", "changed": N, "tracked": N, "untracked": N} and state the survey in prose.

body.name: P2 - Attribute contended files to entries
P2a - Index the Unreleased entries
body.instructions:
Build the entry index that drives the whole release. Read-only.

Run `python3 scripts/release_plan.py index --ledger {{var.ledger}} --json`. It is deterministic and release-agnostic: it extracts the '## [Unreleased]' section of CHANGELOG.md (everything up to the next '## [' header), treats every '- ' item as one entry, and records for each a stable entry_id (a slug of the bolded lead sentence - it is unique and stable, since the commit loop keys its roster on it), the '### ' heading it sits under, a short title, and every repository path named in backticks inside it (brace groups expanded).

It then cross-references those path lists against the actual `git status --porcelain` set and partitions every CHANGED path into exactly one bucket:
  - claimed: named by exactly one entry
  - contended: named by two or more entries (its hunks must be split between them)
  - unclaimed: named by no entry
Paths an entry names that are not actually changed are reported as dropped_citations - a few are normal, but a large count means the changelog is describing a different tree. Entries whose cited files are all absent are listed as entries_without_live_paths: their work already shipped, so the commit loop must not expect a commit for them.

Read the output and sanity-check it - the entry count against the section, the contended list against what you would expect from the entries. Do NOT re-derive the partition by hand; the script's output is the record, and a hand-built index that disagrees with it is exactly what a resume would then have to reconcile.

The script has already written the full index to {{var.ledger}} under 'entry_index' (entries, claimed, contended, unclaimed, dropped_citations, entries_without_live_paths). Then emit_artifact a data part named "contended" holding {"files": [<contended paths>]} - this exact list drives the fan-out below, so it must be a JSON array of path strings and nothing else. Finally state in prose the four bucket sizes and the entry count.

body.name: P2b - Split each contended file's hunks
Attribute the hunks of one file
body.instructions:
You are attributing the hunks of ONE file to the changelog entries that claim it. Your file is: {{item}}

This stage is read-only with respect to git. Do NOT stage, commit, or touch the index - five siblings are running concurrently and the index is a single shared resource. You write patch files; a later serial stage applies them.

1. Read 'entry_index' from {{var.ledger}} and collect every entry whose path list names {{item}}. That set is your target set.
2. Run `python3 scripts/release_hunks.py dump {{item}}` for a numbered hunk listing (index, header, first changed lines), and `git diff -- {{item}}` for the full text whenever the listing's few lines are not enough to attribute a hunk. The hunk indices the listing prints are the keys you will record in step 4.
3. Read each entry's changelog text. Attribute every hunk to exactly one entry, using what the entry says it changed. If a hunk genuinely carries two entries' changes in the same lines, assign it to the entry whose claim is load-bearing for it and record that decision explicitly - it is the one legitimate reason two entries share a commit.

MERGE ESCAPE - take it rather than guessing, but prefer a split. If you cannot attribute this file's hunks to its claiming entries with confidence - the entries describe genuinely interleaved work, or the change is a wholesale rewrite with no per-entry seam - do NOT invent a split. Write no patch files for it and instead run `python3 scripts/release_hunks.py merge --file {{item}} --entries <every entry_id that claims it, comma-separated> --reason "<the specific obstacle>" --out {{var.patch_dir}}`, which writes {{var.patch_dir}}/_merges/<flattened-path>.json holding {"file": ..., "entry_ids": [...], "reason": ...} and refuses a generic reason. Those entries then share ONE commit. A recorded merge is worse history than a correct split and better history than a wrong one: a mis-split yields a clean commit whose subject names work it does not contain, and nothing downstream can ever detect that, whereas a merge is counted, reasoned, and visible in the plan. The reason must name what blocked the split - "hard to tell" is not a reason, and a merge asserted without one will be rejected by the plan stage.
4. Record the attribution as data, not as diff text: write {{var.attrib_dir}}/<flattened-path>.json mapping EVERY hunk index from the dump to an entry_id, e.g. {"0": "<entry_id>", "1": "<entry_id>", "2": "<entry_id>"}. (<flattened-path> is the file path with every '/' replaced by '__'.) Do not hand-write patch files - a hand-written diff is where line-count and context errors come from.
5. Run `python3 scripts/release_hunks.py split --file {{item}} --attrib {{var.attrib_dir}}/<flattened-path>.json --out {{var.patch_dir}}`. It writes {{var.patch_dir}}/<entry_id>/<flattened-path>.patch for each entry that got at least one hunk - the file's diff header plus ONLY that entry's hunks, headers left exactly as git produced them (git apply tolerates the offsets that dropping neighbouring hunks introduces) - and then validates every patch with `git apply --cached --check`, the form that validates without touching the index, which is what makes it safe to run here. It refuses an attribution that leaves a hunk unmapped or names a hunk that does not exist, and a patch that fails --check is a real error: report it and fail.

emit_artifact each patch file with group="attr-{{item}}" and a label naming its entry_id, plus a text part named "attribution" in the same group listing hunk-count-per-entry. Then state in prose how many hunks went to which entry, and flag any hunk you could not attribute confidently.

body.name: P3a - Batch the unclaimed files
body.instructions:
Batch the unclaimed paths that still need a verdict. Read-only. Do NOT build the batches by hand: a hand-built batching dropped 25 paths and duplicated 8 on 2026-10-10, which made the commit-plan gate refuse.

Run `python3 scripts/release_plan.py batches --ledger {{var.ledger}} --triage-dir {{var.triage_dir}} --size 15`. It takes entry_index.unclaimed, skips every path that already carries a verdict in some {{var.triage_dir}}/batch-*.json (so a rerun triages only what is missing), and prints {"batches": [{"id": ..., "paths": [...]}], "pending": N, "triaged": M}. Each path appears in exactly one batch, and each batch's id is a hash of its paths, so batch files cannot overwrite an earlier run's verdicts.

emit_artifact a data part named "unclaimed" holding exactly the script's {"batches": [...]} array, unmodified - an empty array when nothing is pending, so the fan-out below runs zero iterations. Then state the pending and already-triaged counts in prose.

body.name: Triage a batch of unclaimed files
body.instructions:
Classify each file in this batch. Your batch is: {{item.paths}}

Read-only with respect to git. Do not stage or commit anything.

For each path, apply the EXCLUSION RULE from your standing context and assign exactly one disposition:
  - assign: it belongs to an existing Unreleased entry that failed to cite it (name the entry_id). Check 'entry_index' in {{var.ledger}} for a plausible owner - a test file usually belongs with the source change it covers.
  - new_entry: it is a real user-visible change with no entry. DRAFT the changelog entry text and the '### ' category it belongs under, but do NOT write it into CHANGELOG.md - a later single stage owns that file, and concurrent writes to it would interleave.
  - exclude: in-progress work. Record a one-line reason.

Before excluding any untracked module, grep the committed tree for its module path and bare filename, including `require(...)` and `import` forms under frontend/src. If committed code references it, it is 'assign' or 'new_entry', never 'exclude' - a committed reference to an uncommitted module breaks a clean checkout at build time even when wrapped in try/catch.

Write your verdicts to {{var.triage_dir}}/batch-{{item.id}}.json as {"verdicts": [{"path": ..., "disposition": ..., "entry_id": ..., "draft_entry": ..., "category": ..., "reason": ...}]}. Do NOT write the shared ledger - siblings are running and would clobber each other; the reconcile stage merges these files.

emit_artifact that file, plus a text part named "triage" summarizing the disposition counts. Then state in prose anything you were unsure about and which way you resolved it.

body.name: P4a - Reconcile the commit plan
body.instructions:
Merge everything the analysis stages produced into ONE commit plan, and refuse to proceed if it does not cover the release. This is the gate: every later stage trusts this plan.

1. Read 'entry_index' and 'release' from {{var.ledger}}.
2. Read every {{var.triage_dir}}/batch-*.json. Fold 'assign' verdicts into their entry's file list. Turn each 'new_entry' verdict into its own group, carrying the drafted entry text forward in the plan so the changelog stage can write it. Collect 'exclude' verdicts into the exclusion list with their reasons.
3. List {{var.patch_dir}} and attach each entry's patch files to its group.
4. Build the groups. A group is {entry_id, entry_ids, subject, files, patches, mode, merge_reasons}. 'entry_ids' names every entry the group satisfies; 'entry_id' is the first of them and is the group's own identity for the commit loop's roster. Normally the list holds one element and the two agree.

MERGES. Read every {{var.patch_dir}}/_merges/*.json the attribution stage wrote. Each names a set of entries that must share a commit because their file had no available split. Fold each such set into ONE group whose 'entry_ids' is the union, and carry the reasons into 'merge_reasons'. A merged group's subject must name every change it carries rather than picking one entry's claim and dropping the others - so it will need a comma, and the SUBJECT TEST below cannot be satisfied by splitting it, because the split is precisely what was unavailable. That comma is the visible cost of the merge and is the one case where it is allowed. Refuse any merge record whose reason does not name a specific obstacle. 'mode' is "patch" when the group has patch files (stage those, then any whole files it also owns) or "whole" when it owns its files outright. 'subject' is a Conventional Commit subject (feat/fix/refactor/docs/chore/test).

SUBJECT TEST - apply it to every subject before recording it. Read the subject and stop at its first comma or semicolon. If what follows names a DIFFERENT change, split the group there and repeat. Listing the files one change touched is fine; listing several changes is not.

HARD GATES - fail this block, with the numbers, if any hold:
  - some Unreleased '- ' entry appears in no group's 'entry_ids'. This is the real invariant and it replaces comparing counts: an entry in no group silently will not ship, whereas a group count below the entry count is legitimate once merges are recorded. Report entry count, group count and merged-entry count as three separate numbers so the shape of the release is visible in the run output rather than only in git log weeks later.
  - some entry appears in more than one group's 'entry_ids'. Two commits would each claim to satisfy it and neither would be the record.
  - more than half the entries are in merged groups. Past that point attribution did not do its job and the run would produce a history no better than the omnibus commits this card exists to replace. Stop and let a human look rather than proceeding - this gate is what keeps the merge escape an escape instead of a default.
  - any changed path appears in no group and no exclusion. A path in neither is a path that silently will not ship.
  - any path appears in more than one group's whole-file list (patch-mode sharing is expected; whole-file sharing means two commits would fight over it).

Write the plan to {{var.ledger}} under 'commit_plan'. Then emit_artifact a data part named "commit_plan" holding {"groups": [{"entry_id": ..., "subject": ..., "files": [...], "patches": [...], "mode": ...}]} - and every group in that array must carry its 'entry_ids' list and, where it is a merge, its 'merge_reasons', because this artifact IS the roster the commit loop iterates and a field omitted here does not exist downstream. Then state the three counts (entries, groups, merged entries) as an explicit ratio, so a coarse grouping is visible in the run output rather than only in git log weeks later.

body.name: P4b - One commit per entry (serial)
body.improve_criterion: every roster group produced exactly one commit containing exactly its own files, with no group skipped and no unrelated file swept in

body.name: Commit one group
body.instructions:
Create exactly ONE commit for this group and verify it landed. Your group is: {{item}}

You are iteration {{index}} of a SERIAL loop. Earlier iterations have already committed; the index is shared, so leave it clean when you finish.

1. Read {{var.ledger}}. If every one of this group's 'entry_ids' is already in 'groups_done', or none of its files appear in `git status --porcelain`, it is already committed: say so, change nothing, and succeed. Never re-commit.
2. Confirm the index is empty (`git diff --cached --name-only`). If a previous iteration left it dirty, that is a real error - report it and fail rather than committing someone else's staged work into your commit.
3. For each file, run `git check-ignore <file>` first. Skip any gitignored path - report it, do not force-add it, and do not treat it as an error.
4. Stage:
   - mode "patch": for each patch file, `git apply --cached --check <patch>` and only then `git apply --cached <patch>`. The --check pass first is what keeps a bad patch from half-staging, because you have no unstage grant to recover with.
   - mode "whole": `git add <file>` for each, or `git rm` for a deletion.
5. Verify the staged set is EXACTLY what the group claims: `git diff --cached --name-only`. If it names a file the group does not own, stop and fail - do not commit and do not attempt to clean up.
6. Commit with the group's subject. Add a body only if the subject needed a qualifier.
7. Verify: `git log -1 --stat`. Confirm the commit exists and contains the expected files. Merely having run git commit is not evidence it landed.
8. Append EVERY id in this group's 'entry_ids' to 'groups_done' in {{var.ledger}} and write it back. A merged group satisfies several entries with one commit, so recording only its primary id would leave the others looking unshipped to the residue sweep, which would then try to commit them again and find nothing to stage.

emit_artifact a text part named "commit" holding the commit subject, its hash, and its file list. Then state in prose what you committed and confirm the index is clean. Do not end on a bare tool call.

body.name: P5 - Account for every remaining change
body.until_condition: every path the commit plan assigned to a group is now committed, and every path still showing as modified or untracked is present in the exclusion list with a stated reason

body.name: Sweep the residue
body.instructions:
Close the gap between what the plan promised and what the tree shows. The exit condition is NOT a clean working tree - excluded in-progress work legitimately stays uncommitted. It is that every remaining path is accounted for.

1. Run `git status --porcelain`. Read 'commit_plan', 'groups_done' and 'exclusions' from {{var.ledger}}.
2. Partition what remains:
   - a path the plan assigned to a group that is NOT committed: the group was missed. Stage exactly that group's files and commit them with the planned subject, verifying with `git log -1 --stat` as the commit loop does.
   - a path in no group and no exclusion list: it was never triaged. Triage it now per the EXCLUSION RULE and either commit it as its own group or add it to 'exclusions' with a reason.
   - a path already excluded with a reason: leave it alone. This is the expected steady state.
3. Update {{var.ledger}} and state, path by path, what is now committed and what remains excluded and why.

If you make no progress on an iteration - the same paths remain unaccounted for and you have no new action to take - say so plainly rather than restating the previous pass. A stalled loop is detected from repeated non-progress, and an honest report of being stuck is more useful than a reworded one.

emit_artifact a text part named "residue" listing the still-uncommitted paths with their reasons.

body.name: P6 - Consolidate the changelog
body.instructions:
Rewrite the '## [Unreleased]' section so it is complete and correctly structured. You are the only stage that writes CHANGELOG.md, which is why the drafted entries from triage were carried in the plan instead of being written as they were found.

1. Read the current '## [Unreleased]' section, and read 'commit_plan' from {{var.ledger}} for every group carrying a drafted entry.
2. Fold each drafted entry in. Cross-check the committed set (`git log <last_released_tag>..HEAD --stat`) against the section: every committed file change should map to at least one entry, and every entry should correspond to real changes. Remove entries for work that was reverted or superseded.
3. Re-emit the whole section with ONE heading block per category. Draft all entries first without committing to placement, bucket them by category, then emit a single '### Added' block containing every Added entry, then a single '### Fixed' block, then '### Changed', in that fixed order. Omit empty headings. A non-standard category gets its own single block, not an interleave.
4. Scan the rendered section top to bottom and verify no '### ' heading text repeats. A repeat means entries were left scattered and must be merged into the earlier occurrence. Report the heading list you ended with as evidence you checked.

Do NOT touch any numbered version section - those are published. Do not rename '## [Unreleased]' yet; the version stage does that.

emit_artifact the file, plus a text part named "headings" listing the final heading order and each one's entry count. Then state what you folded in and what you removed.

body.name: P7 - Bump the version and finalize the changelog
body.instructions:
Apply the target version and close out the changelog section.

1. Read target_version from 'release' in {{var.ledger}}. Do not recompute it - P1 already decided it under the VERSION RULE and a second derivation could disagree.
2. Run `python bump-version.py <TARGET>`. If the files already hold the target this is close to a no-op, which is expected on the honored-human-bump branch - proceed regardless.
3. In CHANGELOG.md: replace '## [Unreleased]' with '## [<TARGET>] - <today's date, YYYY-MM-DD>', then insert a fresh empty '## [Unreleased]' section above it with stub headings '### Added', '### Fixed', '### Changed'.
4. Stage the version files and CHANGELOG.md and commit as `chore: bump version to <TARGET>`. Verify with `git log -1 --stat` that the commit contains the version files and the changelog.

emit_artifact a text part named "bump" holding the target version and the commit hash. Then state which version files changed.

body.name: P8 - Tag
body.instructions:
Create the annotated tag for this release.

Read target_version from 'release' in {{var.ledger}}. Check `git tag -l v<TARGET>` first - if the tag already exists this run is a resume past this point, so report that and succeed without re-tagging. Otherwise run `git tag -a v<TARGET> -m "v<TARGET>"` and confirm with `git tag -l v<TARGET>`.

emit_artifact a text part named "tag" holding the tag name, then state whether you created it or found it already present.

body.name: P9 - Push
body.instructions:
Push the release. This is the point of no return, so verify before and after.

1. Confirm the working tree holds no in-scope uncommitted change: `git status --porcelain`. Anything remaining must already be in 'exclusions' in {{var.ledger}} - if something is not, fail rather than pushing an incomplete release.
2. Run `git push`, then `git push --tags`.
3. Confirm with `git status -sb` that the branch is no longer ahead of upstream, and with `git tag -l v<TARGET>` that the tag exists. If either check fails, the push did not land: fail this block. Do not merely report it - the announce stages are gated on this block's verdict, and a narrated failure that leaves the block succeeded is how a release that never reached the remote got announced.
4. Only now delete {{var.ledger}}'s incomplete markers - set mode to 'pushed' and record 'pushed': {"tag": "v<TARGET>", "head": <`git rev-parse HEAD`>}. An unpushed release is still incomplete, and a ledger cleared too early loses the resume path.

emit_artifact a text part named "push" holding the pushed ref and tag. Then state the result. A failed push is a real error - fail the block.

body.name: P10a - GitHub Release
body.instructions:
PUSH GATE - run this first, and if it fails post NOTHING. Read target_version from 'release' in {{var.ledger}}, then verify from git, not from the ledger or any earlier stage's prose: (a) `git tag -l v<TARGET>` lists the tag; (b) `git status -sb` shows the branch is NOT ahead of its upstream; (c) `git log -1 --format=%s` is `chore: bump version to <TARGET>`. Additionally require mode == 'pushed' in {{var.ledger}}. If ANY of these fails, state which one, create no release, and fail this block. Announcing a release that is not on the remote is the one failure this stage cannot have, and the structural stop on the enclosing group cannot be relied on alone - it only fires if the push stage marked itself failed.

Publish the GitHub Release from the tag. Best-effort: if `gh` fails, report the failure clearly and do not retry indefinitely - the next stage can proceed without you.

1. Read target_version from 'release' in {{var.ledger}}.
2. Extract the changelog body for this version: everything between the '## [<TARGET>]' header and the next '## [' header. Write it to /tmp/ziya-release-notes.md.
3. Run: gh release create v<TARGET> --repo {{var.repo}} --title "v<TARGET>" --notes-file /tmp/ziya-release-notes.md --latest --verify-tag

emit_artifact a text part named "release_url" holding https://github.com/{{var.repo}}/releases/tag/v<TARGET>, then state whether the release was created.

body.name: P10b - Announce in Slack
body.instructions:
PUSH GATE - run this first, and if it fails post NOTHING to any channel. Read target_version from 'release' in {{var.ledger}}, then verify from git, not from the ledger or any earlier stage's prose: (a) `git tag -l v<TARGET>` lists the tag; (b) `git status -sb` shows the branch is NOT ahead of its upstream; (c) `git log -1 --format=%s` is `chore: bump version to <TARGET>`. Additionally require mode == 'pushed' in {{var.ledger}}. If ANY of these fails, state which one, post nothing, and fail this block. A Slack announcement of a release whose commits never landed is the failure this gate exists to prevent; the previous stage's GitHub Release result is irrelevant to it (that stage is best-effort and may legitimately have failed).

Post the release announcement. Best-effort: if Slack posting fails, report it and stop.

FIRST load the `release-announcement` skill with get_skill_details and follow it. It defines the aggregate/filter/rank procedure, the length caps, the per-channel voice and the Slack mrkdwn dialect. Do not improvise a format without loading it.

Gather: the changelog section for this version, `git diff --stat <last_released_tag>..HEAD` (a new top-level module is a candidate headline - it is what distinguishes a new platform from a feature built on one), `git log <last_released_tag>..HEAD --oneline | wc -l` for the commit count, and the release URL from the previous stage ({{previous_sibling.outputs.release_url}}).

Post, in order:
1. #ziya-dev: `v<TARGET> pushed to public :thread:`
2. #ziya-dev CHANNEL (not the thread): the highlights message per the skill, ending with the release link. ONE TITLE PER ITEM, <=70 chars, each line stating one change and stopping. There is NO cap on the number of lines - every significant user-observable item gets one, so a large release is a long list of short titles and that is correct output. Do not select, drop or merge distinct items to shorten it. Order strictly by IMPACT on what a user experiences, never by category - the Added/Fixed label is a prefix, not a sort key. A title is REWRITTEN, not truncated: the changelog's bolded lead is not already a title, and cutting one at its first comma can leave a claim that is narrower than the truth. If the list exceeds ~3500 chars, continue in thread replies in impact order and end the channel message with `... +N more in thread`.
3. #ziya-dev thread (replying to message 1): a link to https://github.com/{{var.repo}}/commits/v<TARGET> plus any overflow titles. Do NOT paste commit hashes inline and do NOT post or attach the changelog section in any form - one version's section runs tens of thousands of characters here and is unreadable in a thread even as a file. The title list in step 2 is already the complete inventory.

Do NOT post to #ziya-interest. That channel announces AVAILABILITY, and nothing is installable at tag-push time - the separate `release` task owns that announcement.

Before posting, count: the number of title lines must equal the number of '- ' items in the changelog section, minus any merged as facets of one change and any cut by the audience gate. State that arithmetic - an unexplained shortfall means items were silently dropped, which is the one failure this surface cannot have.

emit_artifact a text part named "announcement" holding the posted title list, then state the per-channel result you actually observed.
